_note: Original Practice questions aligned with CS Navigator's original Learn lesson for this topic.

questions.title: Exceptions practice 1
choices: ValueError
TypeError
KeyError
FileNotFoundError
questions.explanation: The argument is a string, which is an accepted input type, but its contents do not represent a whole integer. That makes the value invalid.

questions.title: Exceptions practice 2
questions.prompt: Which block runs after try whether an exception occurred or not?
choices: finally
except
else
raise
questions.explanation: `finally` is reserved for work required on both paths. An except block needs a matching failure, while else requires success.

questions.title: Trace Exceptions
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
accepted: Credits must be a whole number
questions.explanation: Only conversion is protected, and only ValueError is handled. The response matches the failure the program understands. The resulting output is 'Credits must be a whole number'.

questions.title: Exceptions practice 5
questions.prompt: Why catch `ValueError` here rather than the broad `Exception`?
choices: So an unrelated bug like a NameError is not hidden behind "Bad number"
Because Exception cannot be used in an except clause
Because ValueError is faster to catch
Because int() can only raise ValueError
questions.explanation: `int(raw)` raises `ValueError` on bad text, so that is the case the message describes. Catching `Exception` would also swallow a NameError or a typo elsewhere in the block and mislabel it as bad input. The narrow catch keeps unrelated bugs visible. It is about correctness, not speed.

questions.title: Empty except risk
questions.prompt: What is risky about writing an empty `except` block?
choices: It can hide the failure and let the program continue with bad or incomplete work.
It catches only syntax errors, so runtime errors still show.
It automatically fixes the failed operation before continuing.
It makes Python retry the same line until it succeeds.
questions.explanation: An empty handler gives no clue about what failed and no recovery action. The program may continue as if the work succeeded when it did not. A useful handler catches an expected problem and responds with a message, fallback, retry, or re-raise.

questions.title: Small try blocks
questions.prompt: Only the `int(text)` conversion is expected to fail. How should the `try` block be shaped?
choices: Wrap the entire program so every bug becomes the same message.
Wrap the smallest operation that can raise the expected error.
Put unrelated print statements inside the handler.
Avoid `try` completely and let user input crash every time.
questions.explanation: A smaller `try` block makes it clear which operation is being protected. If too much code is inside, the handler may catch an unrelated bug and diagnose it incorrectly. That makes debugging harder and can hide real mistakes.

questions.title: Specific exception type
questions.prompt: A menu reads a number with `int(choice)`. Which exception should the handler usually catch?
choices: `Exception`, because broad handlers are always clearer.
`SyntaxError`, because the user typed text.
`ValueError`, because conversion fails when the text is not a valid integer.
`TypeError`, because all input starts as a string.
questions.explanation: `int("abc")` raises ValueError because the value cannot be interpreted as an integer. Catching that specific error documents the expected failure. A broad `Exception` handler can swallow unrelated problems that the program should not pretend to handle.

questions.title: Recovery path
questions.prompt: After catching invalid user input, what should the program do next?
choices: Continue as if the invalid value had been accepted.
Hide the error and skip every later calculation.
Print a traceback to the user and end immediately every time.
Give a clear message, ask again, or use a safe fallback.
questions.explanation: Catching an exception is only useful if the code has a plan for what happens next. For user input, that plan is often a friendly message and another chance to enter a value. Without a recovery path, the handler only hides the problem.

questions.title: Do not hide bugs
questions.prompt: Why should code avoid catching every possible exception around a large block?
choices: It can hide programming mistakes that should be fixed, not treated as expected input problems.
Python refuses to run any code with a broad handler.
A broad handler only catches file errors, not math or type errors.
Broad handlers make every failing line retry automatically.
questions.explanation: Some failures are expected situations, like a missing file or invalid input. Others are bugs, like a misspelled variable or wrong data shape. Catching everything makes those cases look the same and can keep broken logic alive.

questions.title: Finally for cleanup
choices: When code should run only if no exception occurred.
When cleanup should happen whether the `try` block succeeds or fails.
When the handler needs to choose which exception type to catch.
When Python should ignore all errors from the `try` block.
questions.explanation: `finally` runs after the `try` and any matching `except`, no matter which path happened. That makes it a good place for cleanup that must happen either way. It is not a substitute for choosing a specific handler or writing a recovery plan.
